text: Kikukawa Eizan studied first with his father Eiji, a minor painter of the Kanō school, and then with Suzuki Nanrei of the Shijō school. He may also have studied with Totoya Hokkei. In the 1830s he produced many woodblock prints of beautiful women, then gave up printmaking for painting. He was the most prolific, longest-lived and ultimately the best of the late followers of Utamaro who tried to carry on his bijin style. Do not confuse him with Harukawa Eizan.

By the later 15th century Rogier van der Weyden had eclipsed Jan van Eyck in popularity. His paintings were exported to Italy and Spain, and he took commissions from Philip the Good and other Burgundian nobles and foreign aristocrats. His surviving works are mainly religious triptychs and altarpieces, plus portraits and diptychs. He began as Roger de la Pasture. His fame lasted until the 17th century. By the mid-18th century he was almost forgotten.

Jan Bulthuis came from Groningen, where he trained under Jurriaan Andriessen as a painter and Johannes Wieringa as a draftsman. He painted landscapes at first, but later concentrated on townscapes and country views. From 1780 he worked in Amsterdam. In 1785 he enrolled at the Stadstekenacademie and won a gold medal there. He made a series of drawings for Adriaan Loosjes's description of the Zaan villages. He died in 1801.

Francesco Bassano the Younger studied with his father Jacopo and worked in the family workshop with his three brothers. He was the eldest son. Francesco moved to Venice, where he ran the branch of the family business, and he was commissioned to paint a series of historical pictures in the Doge's Palace. He was prone to hypochondria. That made his other ailments worse. He died in 1592.

Three separate blocks went into every print by Antonio da Trento: one for the outlines, one for the shadows, and one for the lighter tints. He specialized in chiaroscuro woodcuts, mostly of religious subjects. He probably learned wood engraving from Ugo da Carpi, and later followed Parmigianino and then the School of Fontainebleau. Three documented works are The Beheading of St. Peter and St. Paul, The Tiburtine Sibyl and Psyche Saluted by the People.

Jerome Myers worked briefly as an actor and scene painter before studying art for a year at Cooper Union and then eight years at the Art Students League, mainly with George de Forest Brush. Born in Petersburg, Virginia, he spent his adult life in New York City. He painted the city and its people with sympathy. He helped organize the 1913 Armory Show, which introduced European modernism to America. He also wrote.

Hardly any documents mention Hans Brosamer apart from his prints. He was probably born in Fulda in the late 1490s, was active there from 1536 to 1545, and later worked in Erfurt. His works include over 600 woodcuts, mostly book illustrations, and 38 engravings. Because his engravings are small, he counts among the Little Masters. He also painted half-length portraits of local elites. He died around 1554.

Giovanni Battista Vanni studied under Jacopo da Empoli, Aurelio Lomi and Matteo Rosselli, and then became a disciple of Cristofano Allori. He is better known as an engraver than as a painter. From 1624 to 1632 he lived in Rome, and he went back to Florence after visiting Venice. In 1642 he etched fifteen plates after Correggio's frescoes in the cupola of Parma Cathedral. He also engraved Veronese's Marriage at Cana.

At twenty Joseph Vivien left Lyon for Paris and found work in Charles Le Brun's large atelier. In 1701 the Académie royale accepted him as a pastel portraitist, and his reception pieces, pastel portraits of the sculptor François Girardon and the architect Robert de Cotte, are in the Louvre. He was made counsellor to the Academy and housed at the Gobelins. He visited Brussels and worked in Munich as first painter to a brother of the Elector of Cologne.

Adriaan de Lelie came from Tilburg and trained with A. Peeters, who painted ornaments, and then with Andreas Bernardus de Quertenmont in Antwerp. In Düsseldorf he copied many portraits by Rubens and Van Dyck. On Professor Camper's advice he settled in Amsterdam. He painted a great number of portraits and cabinet pictures, including one of the art lover Jan Gildemeester showing his collection to a party. His Drawing Academy of the Felix Meritis Society is one of his best.

In 1846 John Mix Stanley showed a gallery of 85 of his paintings in Cincinnati and Louisville. He grew up in the Finger Lakes region of New York and started by painting signs and portraits. In 1842 he went to the American West to paint Native American life. In the Mexican–American War he joined Colonel Kearney's expedition to California and painted the campaign, and later the Oregon Territory. A big exhibit followed at the Smithsonian. It held over 150 works.

Tawaraya Sōtatsu is best known for decorating calligraphic works by his partner Hon'ami Kōetsu. His folding screens are spectacular and highly influential, and two of them, Wind God and Thunder God, are National Treasures. He also painted the Sekiya and Miotsukushi chapters of The Tale of Genji. He popularized tarashikomi. In that technique a second layer of paint goes on before the first dries. With Kōetsu he is credited with co-founding the Rinpa school.

Pietro della Vecchia was once incorrectly called Pietro Muttoni. He worked in many genres between late Mannerism and early Baroque: altarpieces, portraits, genre scenes and grotesques. He also made pastiches of the leading Italian painters of the 16th century. He designed cartoons for mosaics and restored art, and collectors sought him out as an expert and for valuations of artworks. He lived mostly in Venice.

Very little documentation of Simone Martini's life survives, and art historians debate many attributions. He is thought to have been a pupil of Duccio. Vasari said he was a pupil of Giotto instead, and went with him to Rome. His brother-in-law was the artist Lippo Memmi, and Gombrich said he was a friend of Petrarch. He greatly influenced the International Gothic style. He came from Siena and died in 1344.

Two folding screens by Ogata Kōrin are registered National Treasures: Irises, and Red and White Plum Blossoms. He also decorated round fans, writing boxes and medicine cases. His brother Kenzan made the ceramics and lacquerware that he painted. He is credited with reviving the Rinpa school of painting, fifty years after Hon'ami Kōetsu founded it. He worked as a lacquerer too. He died in 1716.

George Auriol made magazine covers, book illustrations, sheet music, monograms and trademarks, and he also wrote poems and songs. Eugène Grasset introduced him to typography and book design after he arrived in Paris in 1883. Georges Peignot then appointed him to create the Auriol typeface for the Peignot foundry. It was inspired by Art Nouveau. Publishers such as Francis Thibaudeau used it. His real name was Jean-Georges Huyot.

Adam Elsheimer painted small oils on copper, the cabinet paintings, with a variety of light effects and a new way of treating landscape. He had a short career in Rome, and his few works were very influential. Rembrandt and Rubens were among those he influenced. He was one of ten children of a master tailor in Frankfurt. His father's house, near the church that held Dürer's Heller Altarpiece, was destroyed by bombs in 1944. He died in 1610.

Julian Onderdonk is often called the father of Texas painting. His father Robert and his sister Eleanor were painters too. As a teenager in San Antonio he got some training from the Texas artist Verner Moore White. He was an enthusiastic sketcher from boyhood. Onderdonk attended the West Texas Military Academy. He painted Texas Impressionist landscapes and lived from 1882 to 1922.

Jacobus van Looy lost his mother at five, and when his carpenter father died soon after, he ended up in the municipal orphanage in Haarlem. He trained as a house painter but managed to follow drawing classes, from 1877 at the Rijksacademie in Amsterdam. In 1884 he won the Prix de Rome. He then travelled through Italy, Spain and Morocco. He wrote as well as painted.

Giuseppe De Nittis grew up in the wealthiest district of Barletta, near the Corso Vittorio Emanuele, around the corner from the birthplace of the painter Geremia Discanno. He became one of the most important Italian painters of the 19th century. His work merges Salon art with Impressionism. His Paris pictures include the Avenue du Bois de Boulogne and the Arc de Triomphe. He died young, in 1884.

A gamekeeper's son from near Dorfen, Johann Georg von Dillis was educated in Munich with support from the prince-elector of Bavaria. He was trained for the priesthood first, but his real interest was art, and by 1786 he taught drawing at court. In 1790 he became inspector of the Hofgarten Galerie. He kept a curatorial role at the Bavarian court for much of his career, which left him freedom to travel. He first went to Italy in 1794.

At fifteen Jan Adam Kruseman went to Amsterdam and enrolled at the Tekenacademie, where his cousin Cornelis Kruseman gave him his first lessons. He studied in Brussels with François-Joseph Navez and Jacques-Louis David. At twenty-six he became Director of the Academy of Fine Arts. He came from a Haarlem family that produced several well-known artists. He is known mainly for portraits, though he also did landscapes and genre scenes.

Constant Puyo led the Pictorialist movement in France and argued that photography was an artistic medium. He came from a prominent family in Morlaix, and his father Edmond was a painter, amateur archaeologist and mayor in the 1870s. His uncle was the best-selling author Édouard Corbière. For most of his career he was tied to the Photo Club of Paris and served as its president from 1921 to 1926. His photographs appeared in publications worldwide.

Adolf von Becker studied law and drawing at the same time in Helsinki. After he completed his law degree in 1853 he began as a trainee at the Court of Appeals in Turku, still making drawing trips into the countryside. Robert Wilhelm Ekman urged him to study at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts, and he graduated there in 1856. He was one of the first Finnish artists to study in Paris and taught many young artists of the Golden Age of Finnish Art.

Three generations of Protestant pastors came before Johann Friedrich Overbeck in Lübeck, and his father was a burgomaster, poet and mystic. His uncle ran the Gymnasium next to the family mansion. There Johann became a classical scholar and got art lessons. He left in March 1806 for the academy in Vienna under Heinrich Füger. He became a founder of the Nazarene art movement. He died in 1869.

Willem Drost is a mysterious figure, closely linked to Rembrandt, and very few paintings can clearly be attributed to him. He was presumably born in Amsterdam. Houbraken says he studied with Rembrandt and then developed a close working relationship with him. He painted history scenes, biblical compositions, studies of a solitary figure and portraits. His Bathsheba of 1654 was inspired by Rembrandt's. He died young, in 1659.

Theodore Robinson grew up in Evansville, Wisconsin, and briefly studied art in Chicago. In 1874 he went to New York to attend classes at the National Academy of Design. He studied in Paris under Carolus-Duran and Jean-Léon Gérôme, and showed at the 1877 Salon. He visited Giverny and became a close friend of Claude Monet. He was one of the first American artists to take up Impressionism. He died in 1896.

Antonio Visentini, a Venetian, studied under the widely travelled Baroque painter Giovanni Antonio Pellegrini. He made architectural fantasies and capricci, wrote treatises on perspective and was a professor at the Venetian Academy. Today he is best known as the engraver for Canaletto's first great series of Venetian views. The British consul Joseph Smith organized it, and it was begun around 1728 and finished in 1735.

John Opie was the youngest of five children of a master carpenter in Cornwall. By twelve he had mastered Euclid and opened an evening school for poor children. His father did not encourage him and apprenticed him to his own trade of carpentry. But his ability for drawing won out. He became a painter of prominent men and women of his day, including members of the British royal family. He lived from 1761 to 1807.

Nicholas Pocock followed his father to sea and was master of a merchant ship by twenty-six. He became a skilled artist by making ink-and-wash sketches of ships and coastal scenes in his logbooks. In 1778 his employer Richard Champion went bankrupt, hit by the effects of the American Revolutionary War on trade. Pocock gave up the sea and devoted himself to painting. The Royal Academy first exhibited his work in 1782. He specialised in marine art.

A German innkeeper settled in Amsterdam in 1636 with his family, and his son Johannes Lingelbach grew up there. The father ran a labyrinth garden with an astronomical clock and machines that moved or played music and showed biblical or mythological scenes. Johannes lived in Paris from 1642 to 1644, then moved to Lyon, Genoa and Rome. In Rome he worked with several Bentvueghels. He belonged to the second generation of the Bambocciate, genre painters working in Rome.

Haarlem is where Jan Wijnants grew up, the son of a Catholic art dealer who remarried a widow, which made Jan the stepbrother of the painter Egbert van Heemskerck. Jan worked in Haarlem until 1660 and then moved to Amsterdam, where he died. He is mainly known for Italianate landscapes and topographical pictures. Nicolaes de Vree and Adriaen van de Velde trained in his studio. His style later influenced Thomas Gainsborough.

Willy Sluiter came from a family of ministers and grew up in Heerenveen and Zwijndrecht, the son of a notary. He is best known for paintings of Dutch villages and their dwellers. He also painted portraits of Dutch high society, and his work was part of the art competitions at four Olympic Games. He married in 1901 and had a daughter. He lived in Dordrecht and Rotterdam. He died in The Hague.

Ivan Shishkin came from a family of merchants in Yelabuga, and his father traded grain. His grandfather had been a palace peasant who registered as a third-guild merchant in 1792. Shishkin became a Russian Realist painter and draughtsman, best known for landscapes. He was one of the most notable artists to emerge under Tsar Alexander II and one of the founding members of the Peredvizhniki. He lived from 1832 to 1898.

A Pietist pastor, the highest-ranking clergyman in Heilbronn, fathered Heinrich Füger. Füger started training in 1764 with the court painter Nicolas Guibal in Stuttgart. From 1769 he studied in Leipzig with Adam Friedrich Oeser, who had taught Goethe to draw. Italy came next, on a study trip. In 1774 he moved to Vienna, where the English ambassador Robert Murray Keith became his patron. He is a leading German representative of classicism.

Geertruydt Roghman was the oldest sister of Roelant and Magdalena Roghman, and her father was the engraver Henrick Lambertsz Roghman. The painter Roelant Savery was her great-uncle. She probably worked in her father's workshop and left no large body of work in her short life. She is best known for 14 prints after her brother Roelant's sketches, published by Claes Jansz Visscher as Pleasant Landscapes. They sold well for a long time. She died before 1657.

Jules David was known for his illustrations of contemporary Parisian fashions, and they appeared in many books and magazines. He studied with Pierre Duval Le Camus, a pupil of Jacques-Louis David. From 1824 he used his power of observation to make landscapes and interiors in Gothic style for publishers. During the July Monarchy he also published caricatures. He wanted to see the ideals of liberty and the French republic put into practice. He lived from 1808 to 1892.

Quirijn Boel the Younger came from Antwerp, the son of Jan Boel and nephew of Quirijn Boel the Elder. He worked in Antwerp and Brussels. His three children were born in Brussels in the late 1650s, and their godfathers included David Teniers the Younger and Peter Snayers. He is known for engravings after old master paintings. The best known are those he made for Teniers's Theatrum Pictorium. He died in 1668.

Houbraken wrote that Benjamin Cuyp was a pupil of his uncle Jacob, who also taught his own son Aelbert, and that Aelbert had neater brushwork. The RKD says Houbraken got the family wrong. Benjamin and Jacob were both sons of a glass painter from Venlo, and Benjamin learned to paint from his older half-brother Jacob. Dordrecht was his birthplace and where he died. He painted landscapes.

Hugues Merle mostly painted sentimental or moral subjects, and people often compared him with Bouguereau. He came from La Sône and studied with Léon Cogniet. He started showing at the Salon in 1847. Paul Durand-Ruel began buying his paintings in 1862 and introduced him to Bouguereau. Merle won second class prizes and was made Chevalier of the Legion of Honor. He died in 1881.

Antwerp is where Frederik Bouttats the Elder was born and died. He was apprenticed to the painter and art dealer Matthijs Willenhoudt and became a master of the Guild of Saint Luke in 1612. He is known for reproductive prints after famous painters and for portraits. He also had a hand in producing and selling devotional prints. Some landscapes of the garden of Eden in the style of Jan Brueghel have been attributed to him, but attributions among artists named Frederik Bouttats are confused.

Joseph Blackburn seems to have been the son of a painter. He worked mainly in British North America, with a studio in Boston from 1755 until 1765. His patrons included many important early American families, such as the Winthrops and Otises. Back in London in 1763, he painted portraits in southwestern England, Wales and Dublin. About 150 of his portraits survive. He died in 1787.

Jan de Baen lost his parents as a child and lived with his uncle Hinderk Pyman in Emden, a painter who gave him his first lessons. In Amsterdam he was a pupil of Jacob Adriaensz Backer from 1645 to 1648. He worked for Charles II of England during the king's Dutch exile. From 1660 until his death he lived and worked in The Hague. His portraits were popular, and he painted the most distinguished people of his time.

Jan Wildens often painted the landscapes in compositions by Rubens and other leading Flemish Baroque painters. His own realist landscapes have an eye for detail and a serene character. His father died while he was still young, and his mother remarried Cornelis Cock, who later became the father-in-law of the portrait painter Cornelis de Vos. In 1596 he was registered at the Antwerp Guild of St Luke as an apprentice. He died in 1653.

Telemaco Signorini first leaned toward literature, but his father Giovanni, a court painter to the Grand Duke of Tuscany, encouraged him to paint. He enrolled at the Florentine Academy in 1852. By 1854 he was painting landscapes outdoors. A year later he exhibited for the first time, showing paintings inspired by Walter Scott and Machiavelli. He belonged to the Macchiaioli group and died in 1901.

Soup noodles paid for Isidre Nonell's childhood: his parents owned a small but prosperous factory in Barcelona that made them. He went to school in the Sant Pere neighborhood with his friend Joaquim Mir. Nonell became known for expressive portrayals of socially marginalized people in late 19th-century Barcelona. His brushwork is often post-impressionist but darker than that of many contemporaries. He died in 1911.

Some 3,000 engraved portraits of American political, naval and military figures came from John Chester Buttre's steel-plate business. He published The American Portrait Gallery in three volumes, with text by his daughter Lillian. His first drawing lessons came from Hulaniski, a Polish exile living in Auburn, New York. He then turned to portrait painting, but he was better suited to drawing and wood-engraving. He carried on as a general engraver.

Nobody is sure whether Joris van der Haagen was born in Arnhem or Dordrecht, but he started his career in Arnhem. He probably learned from his father, the painter Abraham van der Haagen. In 1639 he moved to The Hague and joined the Guild of St Luke there in 1643. A year later he became an honorary citizen. In 1656 he was a founding member of the Confrerie Pictura. He specialized in landscapes.

Ignacio Zuloaga grew up in a family of armourers. His father Plácido was a metalworker and damascener, and his great-grandfather, the royal armourer, was a friend of Goya. In his youth Ignacio drew and worked in his father's workshop, though his father meant him for commerce, engineering or architecture. His uncle Daniel Zuloaga was an artist too. He was born in Eibar, near the monastery of Loyola, and died in 1945.

Charles Courtney Curran's father taught school in Hartford, Kentucky, but the family left a few months after he was born, when the Civil War began. They settled in Sandusky, Ohio, where his father became superintendent of schools. Charles showed an early aptitude for art and went to study at the McMicken School in Cincinnati in 1881. He is best known for pictures of women in various settings and for leading the Cragsmoor Art Colony.

Daniël Mijtens, known in England as Daniel Mytens the Elder, came from a family of artists in Delft. His father Maerten was an art dealer and saddler from Brussels. He trained in The Hague, possibly in the studio of Michiel van Mierevelt. He was the nephew of the painter Aert Mijtens and the older brother of Isaac Mijtens. He spent the central years of his career working in England as a portrait painter. He died around 1647.

Abraham Casembroot lived in Sicily from 1623 and worked at Messina. He painted landscapes and marine subjects, mostly storms. Occasionally he painted historical events, and three small pictures on copper by him showing scenes from the Passion were in the church of San Gioacchino at Messina until the 1908 earthquake destroyed it. He made a few etchings of the port of Messina. Cornelis Bol made etchings after five of his harbour scenes.

Hon'ami Kōetsu did calligraphy, lacquer, pottery and gardening, and he was a connoisseur of swords and a devotee of the tea ceremony. His works are considered to have inspired the founding of the Rinpa school of painting. He came from a family of sword polishers and connoisseurs who served the imperial court and warlords of the Sengoku period. Robert Hughes of Time Asia wrote that he is a national treasure several times over in Japan. He died in 1637.

Antonio Vivarini, also called Antonio of Murano, probably founded the earliest family of painters descended from glassworkers in Murano. His younger brother Bartolomeo and his son Alvise Vivarini followed him. He first trained with Andrea da Murano, and Gentile da Fabriano influenced his works. His earliest dated picture is an altarpiece in the Accademia from 1440. The latest, in the Vatican Museums, is from 1464. He was probably alive in 1470.

John William Casilear learned engraving from Peter Maverick in New York in the 1820s and then from Asher Durand. He and Durand became friends and both worked as engravers through the 1830s. By the middle of that decade Durand had grown interested in landscape painting through his friendship with Thomas Cole, and he drew Casilear's attention to it. By 1840 Casilear's interest in art was strong enough for him to travel with Durand. He belonged to the Hudson River School.

A pharmacist in Nîmes fathered Gabriel Ferrier. He studied at the École des Beaux-Arts under Ernest Hébert and Isidore Pils, and showed at the Salon in 1869. Two years later he won the Prix de Rome for a scene from the Flood and studied at the French Academy in Rome. Back in France he specialized in portraits of notable figures of the Third Republic. He took a long trip to Algeria.

For five years Oscar Björck studied under Edvard Perséus at the Academy in Stockholm, painting works such as Loki Imprisoned by the Æsir. His Return of the Prodigal Son won the Royal Medal in 1882. A travel scholarship followed. He spent a winter in Paris and the next in Munich, where he painted a few portraits. He later became a professor at the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts. He died in 1929.

Geo Poggenbeek began painting at nineteen, studying first under J. D. Veldhuizen and later at the Amsterdam Rijksakademie. For a while he painted ducks and calves under willows just like Willem Maris. Anton Mauve influenced him more lastingly, and he shared Mauve's soft light tone. His tonality also shows the influence of Boudin, Corot and Jongkind. He travelled to Italy for five years. He stayed close to the Hague School.

Giulio Aristide Sartorio showed a Symbolist work at the 1883 International Exposition of Rome. He befriended Nino Costa and Gabriele D'Annunzio. He won a gold medal at the Paris Universal Exhibition and met the Pre-Raphaelites in England. He took part in the Venice Biennale from its first edition in 1895, and then taught for two years at the Weimar Academy of Fine Arts. He also directed films.

Witold Pruszkowski spent his childhood in Odesa and Kyiv. His family emigrated to Dieppe in 1860, and he moved to Paris, where Tadeusz Gorecki, the son-in-law of Adam Mickiewicz, gave him his first drawing lessons. Later he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich with Alexander von Wagner. Then he studied at the Kraków Academy. He painted in the Symbolist style and died in Budapest in 1896.

Harold Gilman grew up at Snargate Rectory in the Romney Marshes of Kent, where his father was the Rector. He was one of seven children. He went to Abingdon School and Tonbridge School, then spent a year at Brasenose College, Oxford. He painted interiors, portraits and landscapes. He was a founder member of the Camden Town Group. He died in 1919, a day after his birthday.

Cornelis Gerritsz Decker lived all his life in Haarlem. He joined the Haarlem Guild of St Luke in 1643. He may have been related to David Decker, a pupil of Gerrit Claesz Bleker, whose only known artwork was once attributed to Cornelis. Cornelis painted landscapes in the manner of Jacob van Ruisdael. Adriaen van Ostade, Philips Wouwerman and Johannes Lingelbach painted some of the figures in them.

Gerard Hoet learned from his father and brother, who were glass painters, and from Warnard van Rijsen in Zaltbommel. In 1672 he moved to The Hague. The Count of Salis bought paintings at his mother's house, and Hoet went back to paint for him. He travelled with the Count to Rees, where he met the Utrecht painters Jan van Bunnik, Justus Nieuwpoort and Andries de Wit. He painted and engraved. He died in 1733.

Orphaned at six, Jan Stobbaerts was cared for by poor relatives and never went to school. At eight he became an apprentice to a joiner. He grew into a Belgian painter and printmaker known for animals, landscapes, genre scenes and portraits. His dark-brown studio tones and forceful treatment of humble subjects made him a pioneer of Realism and of home-grown Impressionism in Belgium. He came from Antwerp and died in 1914.

Frans Hens was one of the first European artists to paint in Sub-Saharan Africa. He studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of Antwerp from 1872 under Jacob Jacobs. He went to America in 1873 but came back the next year to carry on there. At the Academy he became friends with Theodoor Verstraete. Exhibitions of post-impressionist art at the Cercle Artistique of Antwerp influenced him. He also drew and made prints.

Mikhail Nesterov grew up in a strongly patriarchal merchant family. His father sold cloth and small goods but loved history and literature, so he backed his son's wish to be an artist, though he insisted on practical skills first. In 1874 the boy was sent to Moscow to the Voskresensky Realschule. Nesterov was one of the first exponents of Symbolist art in Russia, linked to the Peredvizhniki and Mir iskusstva. He lived from 1862 to 1942.

Eduardo Rosales was orphaned as a teenager. He was the second son of a minor official in Madrid and studied under Federico de Madrazo at the Real Academia de San Fernando in 1851. In 1857 he went to Rome with friends, with no fellowship, until the government gave him a special stipend. He followed the Italian movement called Purismo and specialized in historical scenes. He died in 1873.

Jean-Jacques Feuchère studied under Jean-Pierre Cortot, and Jacques-Léonard Maillet was one of his own students. He made a relief panel for the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and a bronze Satan, dated 1833, that is in the Louvre. He also made pediment sculpture for a church in Paris and a bronze portrait statue of the Marquis of Stafford, now at Dunrobin Castle. He worked as a sculptor and died in 1852.

Suzuki Jūbei, later Yanagawa Shigenobu, came from Edo and went by several art names, among them Kinsai and Ushōsai. He was first the pupil, then the son-in-law, and finally the adopted son of Katsushika Hokusai. He designed illustrated books, prints and surimono. He lived in the Honjo Yanagawa-chō district. From 1822 to 1825 he worked in Osaka with the gifted block cutter and printer Tani Seikō. Theatrical subjects were his focus.

Étienne Jeaurat is remembered above all for lively street scenes. Orphaned early, he was entrusted by his brother, the engraver Edme Jeaurat, to Nicolas Vleughels, a friend of Watteau. Vleughels took him to Rome for an extended stay and shaped his work. Back in Paris, Jeaurat joined the Royal Academy in 1733. He first showed at the Salon in 1737. He died in 1789.

Knud Bergslien came from Voss. His brother Brynjulf was a sculptor, and his nephew Nils a painter and sculptor. As a painter and art teacher, he often portrayed the lives of Norwegian people, their history and heroes of the past. His best known historical painting is Skiing Birchlegs Crossing the Mountain with the Royal Child. He lived from 1827 to 1908.

At eleven Moritz Daffinger was accepted as an apprentice at the Vienna Porcelain Manufactory, where his father had painted. Later he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts and took painting lessons with Heinrich Füger. He went back to work at the factory as one of its leading painters. From 1809 he painted only portraits, specializing in miniatures on ivory. He was also a sculptor. He died in 1849.

Albert Chmielowski lost a leg as a soldier in the Uprising of 1863 and later became a painter. Then he gave up his art career to serve the homeless and destitute, and founded the Albertine Brothers and Albertine Sisters. He was a Franciscan tertiary. He was the eldest of four children in a family of the szlachta, born near Kraków. He lived from 1845 to 1916.

Alvan Fisher was the fourth of six sons. Around 1805 his family moved to Dedham, Massachusetts, where he worked as a clerk in his brother's store, and he always called Dedham home. At eighteen he decided, with his family's support, to become a painter and apprenticed with John Ritto Penniman in Boston. He painted landscapes and genre scenes. He died in 1863.

Vienna was home to Moritz Coschell, who was born Moritz Kocheles. His family changed its name to Coschell in 1896. He began at the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts with the sculptor Anton Brenek. Then he attended the Academy of Fine Arts, where Franz Rumpler and August Eisenmenger were his main teachers. He also studied with Albert Windisch in Frankfurt. He worked as a painter and illustrator.
